Flask Introduction.exp: Introduction to Flask and its ecosystem.

What is Flask: Flask is a lightweight Python web microframework that gives you just the essentials to build web applications. It's minimal, flexible, and unopinionated — you choose your tools (ORM, template engine, etc.). Flask is built on Werkzeug (WSGI toolkit) and Jinja2 (template engine). It's ideal for small to medium projects, APIs, microservices, and prototypes. The 'micro' in microframework means Flask keeps the core simple but is extensible via extensions.

Application Structure: Flask applications can be structured as a single file or as packages. For larger apps, use the Application Factory pattern with Blueprints. A typical Flask project has: app/ directory (__init__.py factory, models.py, routes/, templates/, static/), config.py, requirements.txt, run.py. Blueprints organize routes into modular components. The app factory pattern allows multiple app instances and better testability. Always keep configuration separate from code.

app = create_app()

if __name__ == '__main__':
    app.run(debug=True)


# app/__init__.py
from flask import Flask
from config import Config

def create_app(config_class=Config):
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.config.from_object(config_class)

    # Register blueprints
    from app.routes.main import bp as main_bp
    app.register_blueprint(main_bp)

    from app.routes.auth import bp as auth_bp
    app.register_blueprint(auth_bp, url_prefix='/auth')

    return app
Configuration: Flask configuration is managed via app.config dictionary. Load from object, file, or environment variables. Flask has built-in configs: DEBUG, TESTING, SECRET_KEY, SERVER_NAME. Common extensions add their own config keys. Use python-decouple or python-dotenv for environment variables. Config classes organize settings by environment (Development, Testing, Production). SECRET_KEY is required for sessions and CSRF protection — always keep it secret in production.

# config.py
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()

basedir = os.path.abspath(os.path.dirname(__file__))

class Config:
    SECRET_KEY = os.environ.get('SECRET_KEY') or 'dev-key-change-in-production'
    SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI = os.environ.get('DATABASE_URL') or \
        'sqlite:///' + os.path.join(basedir, 'app.db')
    SQLALCHEMY_TRACK_MODIFICATIONS = False
    MAIL_SERVER = os.environ.get('MAIL_SERVER', 'smtp.gmail.com')
    MAIL_PORT = int(os.environ.get('MAIL_PORT', 587))
    MAIL_USE_TLS = True
    MAIL_USERNAME = os.environ.get('MAIL_USERNAME')
    MAIL_PASSWORD = os.environ.get('MAIL_PASSWORD')

class DevelopmentConfig(Config):
    DEBUG = True

class ProductionConfig(Config):
    DEBUG = False
    SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI = os.environ.get('DATABASE_URL')

class TestingConfig(Config):
    TESTING = True
    SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI = 'sqlite:///:memory:'


# Usage in factory:
app.config.from_object(config_class)

Request & Response: The request object provides access to all incoming data. request.args (query strings), request.form (form data), request.json (JSON body), request.files (uploads), request.headers, request.cookies, request.method. The response object can be customized: make_response(), set headers, set cookies, set status codes. JSON responses with jsonify(). File uploads handled via request.files with secure_filename for sanitization.
Blueprints: Blueprints organize related routes, templates, and static files into reusable modules. They're like mini-applications within the main app. Create a Blueprint object, define routes with @bp.route(), register with app.register_blueprint(). Blueprints support url_prefix for namespacing, subdomain for multi-subdomain apps, and template_folder/static_folder. Use current_app and url_for with endpoint_name.view_name pattern across blueprints.
Route Decorators: Flask uses the @app.route() decorator to bind URLs to view functions. URL parts can be dynamic with <variable_name> or <converter:variable_name>. Converters: string (default), int, float, path (accepts slashes), uuid. HTTP methods via methods parameter. url_for() generates URLs from endpoint names. The request object contains all incoming data (args, form, json, headers, cookies, files). abort() returns HTTP errors. redirect() redirects to another URL.

Jinja2 Templates: Flask uses Jinja2 as its default template engine. Templates go in the templates/ folder. Use {{ }} for expressions, {% %} for control flow, {# #} for comments. Template inheritance with {% extends %} and {% block %}. Include partials with {% include %}. Special variables: config, request, session, g, url_for, get_flashed_messages. Autoescaping is enabled for .html templates. Filters: safe, capitalize, lower, upper, title, trim, striptags, escape, default, length, join, round, format, truncate.

Static Files: Static files (CSS, JS, images) are served from the static/ folder. Use url_for('static', filename='...') to generate URLs. Flask automatically serves static files in development. In production, use a web server (Nginx) or CDN. Flask-Assets or webpack can bundle and minify assets. Custom static URL path via app's static_url_path. Multiple static folders possible with Blueprint static_folder or via send_from_directory.

Flask-SQLAlchemy: Flask-SQLAlchemy integrates SQLAlchemy ORM into Flask. Install: pip install flask-sqlalchemy. Configure database URI in app.config. Define models as classes inheriting from db.Model. Column types: Integer, String, Text, Boolean, DateTime, Float, ForeignKey. Relationships: db.relationship() for backrefs. Create tables with db.create_all(). Session management is automatic. Flask-Migrate (Alembic) handles schema migrations.

# app/__init__.py — initialization
from flask import Flask
from flask_sqlalchemy import SQLAlchemy
from flask_migrate import Migrate

db = SQLAlchemy()
migrate = Migrate()

def create_app():
    app = Flask(__name__)
    app.config['SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI'] = 'sqlite:///app.db'
    app.config['SQLALCHEMY_TRACK_MODIFICATIONS'] = False

    db.init_app(app)
    migrate.init_app(app, db)

    from app.routes import main, auth
    app.register_blueprint(main.bp)
    app.register_blueprint(auth.bp)

    return app


# app/models.py
from app import db
from datetime import datetime, timezone

class User(db.Model):
    id = db.Column(db.Integer, primary_key=True)
    username = db.Column(db.String(80), unique=True, nullable=False)
    email = db.Column(db.String(120), unique=True, nullable=False)
    password_hash = db.Column(db.String(128))
    created_at = db.Column(db.DateTime, default=lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc))
    posts = db.relationship('Post', backref='author', lazy='dynamic')

    def __repr__(self):
        return f'<User {self.username}>'

class Post(db.Model):
    id = db.Column(db.Integer, primary_key=True)
    title = db.Column(db.String(200), nullable=False)
    body = db.Column(db.Text, nullable=False)
    created_at = db.Column(db.DateTime, default=lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc))
    user_id = db.Column(db.Integer, db.ForeignKey('user.id'), nullable=False)

    def __repr__(self):
        return f'<Post {self.title}>'
CRUD Operations: SQLAlchemy CRUD follows a session-based pattern. Create: db.session.add(obj). Read: Model.query.all(), Model.query.get(id), Model.query.filter_by(). Update: modify object attributes and commit. Delete: db.session.delete(obj). Always call db.session.commit() to persist changes. Query filters: filter(), filter_by(), order_by(), limit(), offset(), first(), first_or_404(), get_or_404(), paginate(). Aggregations with db.func.count(), db.func.sum(). Relationships: user.posts, post.author.

# CRUD operations
from app import db
from app.models import User, Post

# CREATE
user = User(username='alice', email='alice@example.com')
db.session.add(user)
db.session.commit()

post = Post(title='Hello World', body='First post!', author=user)
db.session.add(post)
db.session.commit()

# READ
all_users = User.query.all()
user = User.query.get(1)
user = User.query.filter_by(username='alice').first()
user = User.query.filter(User.email.endswith('@example.com')).all()

# Pagination
page = User.query.paginate(page=1, per_page=20, error_out=False)
page.items  # items on this page
page.total  # total items
page.pages  # total pages
page.has_prev, page.has_next, page.prev_num, page.next_num

# UPDATE
user = User.query.get(1)
user.email = 'alice@newdomain.com'
db.session.commit()

# DELETE
db.session.delete(user)
db.session.commit()

# Relationships
user = User.query.get(1)
user.posts.all()  # all posts by user
post = Post.query.get(1)
post.author.username  # author relationship

# Complex queries
from sqlalchemy import func

# Count posts per user
users_with_counts = db.session.query(
    User.username,
    func.count(Post.id).label('post_count')
).join(Post).group_by(User.id).all()

# Get recent posts with their authors
recent = Post.query.order_by(Post.created_at.desc()).limit(10).all()
Migrations (Flask-Migrate): Flask-Migrate wraps Alembic for database migrations. Initialize with flask db init. Auto-detect model changes with flask db migrate -m 'message'. Apply with flask db upgrade. Rollback with flask db downgrade. View history with flask db history. Check current revision with flask db current. Merge conflicts by editing migration files manually. Always review auto-generated migrations before applying.

# Terminal commands
flask db init                  # Initialize migrations (creates migrations/ folder)
flask db migrate -m 'Add User and Post models'  # Create migration
flask db upgrade               # Apply migration
flask db downgrade             # Rollback last migration
flask db history               # View migration history
flask db current               # Current revision

# Migration file example:
# migrations/versions/abc123_add_user_and_post_models.py
"""Add User and Post models

Revision ID: abc123
Revises:
Create Date: 2024-01-15 10:30:00
"""
from alembic import op
import sqlalchemy as sa

revision = 'abc123'
down_revision = None

def upgrade():
    op.create_table('user',
        sa.Column('id', sa.Integer(), nullable=False),
        sa.Column('username', sa.String(length=80), nullable=False),
        sa.Column('email', sa.String(length=120), nullable=False),
        sa.PrimaryKeyConstraint('id'),
        sa.UniqueConstraint('username'),
        sa.UniqueConstraint('email')
    )
    op.create_table('post',
        sa.Column('id', sa.Integer(), nullable=False),
        sa.Column('title', sa.String(length=200), nullable=False),
        sa.Column('body', sa.Text(), nullable=False),
        sa.Column('user_id', sa.Integer(), nullable=False),
        sa.ForeignKeyConstraint(['user_id'], ['user.id']),
        sa.PrimaryKeyConstraint('id')
    )

def downgrade():
    op.drop_table('post')
    op.drop_table('user')

WTForms: Flask-WTF integrates WTForms for form handling and CSRF protection. Define form classes with fields and validators. Common fields: StringField, PasswordField, BooleanField, SelectField, TextAreaField, FileField, DateField, IntegerField, FloatField, RadioField, SelectMultipleField, HiddenField, SubmitField. Validators: DataRequired, Email, Length, EqualTo, NumberRange, URL, Regexp, AnyOf, Optional. CSRF protection is enabled by default. Render forms manually or with macros.

# app/forms.py
from flask_wtf import FlaskForm
from wtforms import StringField, PasswordField, BooleanField, \
    TextAreaField, SelectField, SubmitField
from wtforms.validators import DataRequired, Email, Length, EqualTo

class RegistrationForm(FlaskForm):
    username = StringField('Username',
        validators=[DataRequired(), Length(min=3, max=80)])
    email = StringField('Email',
        validators=[DataRequired(), Email()])
    password = PasswordField('Password',
        validators=[DataRequired(), Length(min=8)])
    confirm_password = PasswordField('Confirm Password',
        validators=[DataRequired(), EqualTo('password')])
    accept_tos = BooleanField('Accept Terms',
        validators=[DataRequired()])
    role = SelectField('Role', choices=[
        ('user', 'User'), ('editor', 'Editor'), ('admin', 'Admin')
    ])
    submit = SubmitField('Register')

class PostForm(FlaskForm):
    title = StringField('Title',
        validators=[DataRequired(), Length(max=200)])
    body = TextAreaField('Content',
        validators=[DataRequired()])
    category = SelectField('Category', coerce=int)
    submit = SubmitField('Publish')
Form Templates: Forms are rendered in templates with form.field() or manually. CSRF token via form.hidden_tag() or {{ form.csrf_token }}. Flash messages for feedback. Form validation errors displayed per field. Macro-based form rendering reduces repetition. Bootstrap-friendly rendering with formnovalidate for client-side validation can coexist. File upload requires enctype=multipart/form-data on the form.

Flask Data.exp: Working with data and APIs in Flask.

Flask RESTful: Flask-RESTful simplifies API building with Resource classes. Install: pip install flask-restful. Define resources as classes with methods for HTTP verbs (get, post, put, delete, patch). Request parsing with reqparse for validation. Fields marshaling with marshal_with for consistent responses. Alternatively, use Flask's built-in jsonify() and request.get_json() for simpler APIs. Flask-RESTx adds Swagger documentation.

# app/api.py — Flask-RESTful
from flask import Blueprint
from flask_restful import Api, Resource, reqparse, fields, marshal_with
from app.models import Post
from app import db

api_bp = Blueprint('api', __name__, url_prefix='/api/v1')
api = Api(api_bp)

# Request parser
post_parser = reqparse.RequestParser()
post_parser.add_argument('title', type=str, required=True, help='Title is required')
post_parser.add_argument('body', type=str, required=True)
post_parser.add_argument('user_id', type=int, required=True)

# Response fields
post_fields = {
    'id': fields.Integer,
    'title': fields.String,
    'body': fields.String,
    'created_at': fields.DateTime(dt_format='iso8601'),
    'author': fields.String(attribute=lambda x: x.author.username),
}

class PostResource(Resource):
    @marshal_with(post_fields)
    def get(self, post_id=None):
        if post_id:
            return Post.query.get_or_404(post_id)
        return Post.query.all()

    @marshal_with(post_fields)
    def post(self):
        args = post_parser.parse_args()
        post = Post(title=args['title'], body=args['body'], user_id=args['user_id'])
        db.session.add(post)
        db.session.commit()
        return post, 201

    @marshal_with(post_fields)
    def put(self, post_id):
        post = Post.query.get_or_404(post_id)
        args = post_parser.parse_args()
        post.title = args['title']
        post.body = args['body']
        db.session.commit()
        return post

    def delete(self, post_id):
        post = Post.query.get_or_404(post_id)
        db.session.delete(post)
        db.session.commit()
        return '', 204

api.add_resource(PostResource, '/posts', '/posts/<int:post_id>')


# Simpler JSON API without Flask-RESTful
@bp.route('/api/posts', methods=['GET'])
def get_posts():
    posts = Post.query.all()
    return jsonify([{
        'id': p.id,
        'title': p.title,
        'body': p.body,
        'created_at': p.created_at.isoformat(),
        'author': p.author.username
    } for p in posts])

Production Deployment: Flask production deployment uses a WSGI server (Gunicorn, uWSGI) behind a reverse proxy (Nginx). Set debug=False, use a proper SECRET_KEY, configure logging. Environment variables for all secrets. Database migrations applied before starting. Gunicorn with multiple workers for concurrency. Systemd service for process management. Docker containerization is common. Popular platforms: Heroku, Railway, Render, PythonAnywhere, DigitalOcean App Platform.

Flask-Login: Flask-Login manages user sessions. Install: pip install flask-login. User model must implement is_authenticated, is_active, is_anonymous, get_id(). Use login_required decorator to protect views. login_user() logs in a user, logout_user() logs out. current_user proxy provides access to logged-in user. Remember me with remember=True. User loader callback reloads user from session ID. Requires SECRET_KEY for session signing. Flask-Bcrypt for password hashing.
